claims.claim: Torso sequences were identified in deuterostomes, lophotrochozoans, cnidarians and ecdysozoans.
claims.source: We identified torso sequences in deuterostomes, lophotrochozoans, cnidarians and ecdysozoans (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), indicating that the trunk-torso neuropeptide signalling pathway dates back at least as far as the last common ancestor of Cnidaria, Ctenophora and Bilateria and is thus not restricted to Bilateria as suggested previously (e.g., Jékely, 2013) (Figures 2A,B and 4A).
claims.evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The trunk-torso neuropeptide signalling pathway dates back at least as far as the last common ancestor of Cnidaria, Ctenophora and Bilateria.
claims.source: We identified torso sequences in deuterostomes, lophotrochozoans, cnidarians and ecdysozoans (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), indicating that the trunk-torso neuropeptide signalling pathway dates back at least as far as the last common ancestor of Cnidaria, Ctenophora and Bilateria and is thus not restricted to Bilateria as suggested previously (e.g., Jékely, 2013) (Figures 2A,B and 4A).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the phyletic distribution of trunk and torso across these lineages.

claims.claim: The trunk-torso neuropeptide signalling pathway is not restricted to Bilateria.
claims.source: We identified torso sequences in deuterostomes, lophotrochozoans, cnidarians and ecdysozoans (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), indicating that the trunk-torso neuropeptide signalling pathway dates back at least as far as the last common ancestor of Cnidaria, Ctenophora and Bilateria and is thus not restricted to Bilateria as suggested previously (e.g., Jékely, 2013) (Figures 2A,B and 4A).
claims.evidence: This contradicts previous suggestions and is based on the identification of these components in cnidarians and ctenophores.

claims.claim: ETH was first identified as a hormone released in response to decreasing ecdysone levels in insects.
claims.source: In insects, the first hormone released in response to decreasing ecdysone levels is usually ETH (Zitnan et al., 1996; Zitnan et al., 1999) although in the lepidopteran Manduca sexta the neuropeptide corozanin acts as the trigger for the release of ETH from the epitracheal glands (Kim et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on ETH function in insects.

claims.claim: In the lepidopteran Manduca sexta, the neuropeptide corozanin acts as the trigger for the release of ETH from the epitracheal glands.
claims.source: In insects, the first hormone released in response to decreasing ecdysone levels is usually ETH (Zitnan et al., 1996; Zitnan et al., 1999) although in the lepidopteran Manduca sexta the neuropeptide corozanin acts as the trigger for the release of ETH from the epitracheal glands (Kim et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kim et al. (2004).

claims.claim: Knockdown of the eth gene in Drosophila leads to lethality at the expected onset of ecdysis.
claims.source: Knockdown of the eth gene in Drosophila (Park et al., 2002) and of eth and its receptors in Tribolium and Schistocerca (Arakane et al., 2008; Lenaerts et al., 2017) lead to lethality at the expected onset of ecdysis, demonstrating the essential role of the ETH peptidergic signalling system in moulting (Park et al., 2002; Arakane et al., 2008; Lenaerts et al., 2017; Shi et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies on ETH function.

claims.claim: Knockdown of eth and its receptors in Tribolium and Schistocerca leads to lethality at the expected onset of ecdysis.
claims.source: Knockdown of the eth gene in Drosophila (Park et al., 2002) and of eth and its receptors in Tribolium and Schistocerca (Arakane et al., 2008; Lenaerts et al., 2017) lead to lethality at the expected onset of ecdysis, demonstrating the essential role of the ETH peptidergic signalling system in moulting (Park et al., 2002; Arakane et al., 2008; Lenaerts et al., 2017; Shi et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies on ETH function.

claims.claim: The ETH peptidergic signalling system plays an essential role in moulting.
claims.source: Knockdown of the eth gene in Drosophila (Park et al., 2002) and of eth and its receptors in Tribolium and Schistocerca (Arakane et al., 2008; Lenaerts et al., 2017) lead to lethality at the expected onset of ecdysis, demonstrating the essential role of the ETH peptidergic signalling system in moulting (Park et al., 2002; Arakane et al., 2008; Lenaerts et al., 2017; Shi et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the lethality observed when ETH is knocked down.

claims.claim: ETH and its receptor are present in tardigrades and arthropods.
claims.source: Our screening and phylogenetic analyses confirmed the presence of ETH and its receptor in tardigrades and arthropods, thus corroborating previous studies (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Figure 2—source data 2) (Zitnan et al., 1996; Zitnan et al., 1999; Park et al., 2002; Arakane et al., 2008; Veenstra et al., 2012; Lenaerts et al., 2017; Koziol, 2018; Zhu et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is based on the screening and phylogenetic analyses conducted in this study and corroborated by previous studies.

claims.claim: The ETH ligand was only found in insects (Drosophila and Tribolium) among arthropods, but was lacking in the crustacean Parhyale hawaiensis and the arachnid Parasteatoda tepidariorum.
claims.source: For Arthropoda, the ETH ligand was only found in insects (Drosophila and Tribolium), but was lacking in the crustacean Parhyale hawaiensis and the arachnid Parasteatoda tepidariorum.
claims.evidence: This is based on the genomic screening conducted in this study.

claims.claim: Studies on the two mites Panonychus citri and Tetranychus urticae as well as several decapods have shown the presence of the ETH ligand in chelicerates and crustaceans.
claims.source: However, studies on the two mites Panonychus citri and Tetranychus urticae as well as several decapods have shown the presence of the ETH ligand in chelicerates and crustaceans (in which the homology was reconfirmed by our clustering analysis) (Veenstra et al., 2012; Veenstra, 2016; Zhu et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and confirmed by clustering analysis in this study.

claims.claim: The entire ETH signalling pathway was not found in the two onychophoran genomes analysed.
claims.source: Surprisingly, we did not find the entire ETH signalling pathway in the two onychophoran genomes analysed herein (Figures 2B and 4B, Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Figure 2—source data 2).
claims.evidence: This is based on the genomic screening conducted in this study.

claims.claim: Due to the fragmented nature of the onychophoran genomes, a final statement whether the ETH signalling system was indeed lost in this lineage cannot be made at present.
claims.source: Due to the fragmented nature of the onychophoran genomes a final statement whether this signalling system was indeed lost in this lineage cannot be made at present.
claims.evidence: This is a cautious interpretation acknowledging the limitations of the available genomic data.

claims.claim: No eth ortholog was identified outside the panarthropods, including the nematode C. elegans.
claims.source: No eth ortholog was identified outside the panarthropods, including the nematode C. elegans, suggesting that this gene originated in the last common ancestor of Panarthropoda (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is based on the absence of eth in non-panarthropod genomes screened in this study.

claims.claim: The eth gene originated in the last common ancestor of Panarthropoda.
claims.source: No eth ortholog was identified outside the panarthropods, including the nematode C. elegans, suggesting that this gene originated in the last common ancestor of Panarthropoda (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the restriction of eth to panarthropods.

claims.claim: The ETH receptor is present in arthropods (insects, crustaceans and arachnids), mollusks, nemerteans, brachiopods, echinoderms, cephalochordates, vertebrates and acoels.
claims.source: Our findings on the distribution of the ETH receptor are in agreement with the results of previous studies and demonstrate the presence of this receptor in arthropods (insects, crustaceans and arachnids), mollusks, nemerteans, brachiopods, echinoderms, cephalochordates (in which we found a substantial expansion of eth-receptor homologs in the genomes of Branchiostoma floridae and B. belcheri), vertebrates and acoels (Park et al., 2003; Roller et al., 2010; Veenstra et al., 2012; Mirabeau and Joly, 2013; Lenaerts et al., 2017; Thiel et al., 2018; Zhu et al., 2019) (Figures 2B and 4A, Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Figure 2—source data 2).
claims.evidence: This is based on the phylogenetic analysis conducted in this study and corroborated by previous studies.

claims.claim: There is a substantial expansion of eth-receptor homologs in the genomes of Branchiostoma floridae and B. belcheri.
claims.source: Our findings on the distribution of the ETH receptor are in agreement with the results of previous studies and demonstrate the presence of this receptor in arthropods (insects, crustaceans and arachnids), mollusks, nemerteans, brachiopods, echinoderms, cephalochordates (in which we found a substantial expansion of eth-receptor homologs in the genomes of Branchiostoma floridae and B. belcheri), vertebrates and acoels (Park et al., 2003; Roller et al., 2010; Veenstra et al., 2012; Mirabeau and Joly, 2013; Lenaerts et al., 2017; Thiel et al., 2018; Zhu et al., 2019) (Figures 2B and 4A, Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Figure 2—source data 2).
claims.evidence: This is based on the phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: Individual components of the ETH signalling system were present at the base of Bilateria.
claims.source: This provides evidence for the presence of individual components of the ETH signalling system already at the base of Bilateria (Figures 2A and 4A).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the broad distribution of the ETH receptor across bilaterian lineages.

claims.claim: Eclosion hormone (EH) was first identified as a blood-borne factor in three lepidopteran species, Hyalophora cecropia, Antheraea polyphemus and Antheraea pernyi.
claims.source: Eclosion hormone (EH) was first identified as a blood-borne factor (Truman and Riddiford, 1970) in three lepidopteran species, Hyalophora cecropia, Antheraea polyphemus and Antheraea pernyi.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to the original discovery of EH.

claims.claim: A positive feedback loop between EH and ETH was found in Manduca and suggested in Tribolium.
claims.source: A positive feedback loop between EH and ETH was found in Manduca and suggested in Tribolium (Ewer et al., 1997; Arakane et al., 2008), whereas in Drosophila, EH has been described either acting downstream of ETH (Kim et al., 2006a; Kim et al., 2006b) or in a positive endocrine feedback loop with ETH (Krüger et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on EH-ETH interactions in different insect species.

claims.claim: In Drosophila, EH has been described either acting downstream of ETH or in a positive endocrine feedback loop with ETH.
claims.source: A positive feedback loop between EH and ETH was found in Manduca and suggested in Tribolium (Ewer et al., 1997; Arakane et al., 2008), whereas in Drosophila, EH has been described either acting downstream of ETH (Kim et al., 2006a; Kim et al., 2006b) or in a positive endocrine feedback loop with ETH (Krüger et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to conflicting studies on EH function in Drosophila.

claims.claim: eh knockout in Drosophila melanogaster did not abolish ecdysis, but instead produced flies with discrete behavioural deficits such as slow and uncoordinated eclosion.
claims.source: Despite EH being a key regulator of ecdysis in insects, eh knockout in Drosophila melanogaster did not abolish ecdysis, but instead produced flies with discrete behavioural deficits such as slow and uncoordinated eclosion. This shows that EH is involved, but does not play an essential role, in moulting in these insects (McNabb et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to McNabb et al. (1997).

claims.claim: EH is involved, but does not play an essential role, in moulting in Drosophila.
claims.source: Despite EH being a key regulator of ecdysis in insects, eh knockout in Drosophila melanogaster did not abolish ecdysis, but instead produced flies with discrete behavioural deficits such as slow and uncoordinated eclosion. This shows that EH is involved, but does not play an essential role, in moulting in these insects (McNabb et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that flies can still moult without EH, though with deficits.

claims.claim: The result that EH is not essential for moulting in Drosophila has been contested in a more recent study using eh null mutants.
claims.source: This result, however, has been contested in a more recent study using eh null mutants in Drosophila (Krüger et al., 2015), showing that the lack of eh function is lethal during larval fruit fly ecdysis.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Krüger et al. (2015) showing contradictory results.

claims.claim: The lack of eh function is lethal during larval fruit fly ecdysis.
claims.source: This result, however, has been contested in a more recent study using eh null mutants in Drosophila (Krüger et al., 2015), showing that the lack of eh function is lethal during larval fruit fly ecdysis.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Krüger et al. (2015).

claims.claim: EH has traditionally been considered to be confined to arthropods.
claims.source: Traditionally considered to be confined to arthropods, recent studies showed the presence of EH and its receptor, a guanylyl cyclase, in echinoderms and tardigrades (Zandawala et al., 2017; Koziol, 2018).
claims.evidence: This represents the previous state of knowledge before recent discoveries.

claims.claim: Recent studies showed the presence of EH and its receptor, a guanylyl cyclase, in echinoderms and tardigrades.
claims.source: Traditionally considered to be confined to arthropods, recent studies showed the presence of EH and its receptor, a guanylyl cyclase, in echinoderms and tardigrades (Zandawala et al., 2017; Koziol, 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies expanding the known distribution of EH.

claims.claim: The EH receptor is a guanylyl cyclase.
claims.source: Traditionally considered to be confined to arthropods, recent studies showed the presence of EH and its receptor, a guanylyl cyclase, in echinoderms and tardigrades (Zandawala et al., 2017; Koziol, 2018).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about the EH receptor type.

claims.claim: The presence of the EH ligand extends to cnidarians, acoels, hemichordates, lophotrochozoans (mollusks, annelids, nemerteans and phoronids) and onychophorans.
claims.source: Our study corroborates these findings but considerably expands the presence of the EH ligand to cnidarians, acoels, hemichordates, lophotrochozoans (mollusks, annelids, nemerteans and phoronids) and onychophorans (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, Figure 2—source data 3).
claims.evidence: This is based on the genomic and transcriptomic screening conducted in this study.

claims.claim: All EH ligand orthologs harbour the six cysteine conserved residues except for Cnidaria, in which only five are present.
claims.source: All EH ligand orthologs harbour the six cysteine conserved residues (Zitnan et al., 2007) except for Cnidaria, in which only five are present.
claims.evidence: This is based on sequence analysis of EH orthologs identified in this study.

claims.claim: The identification of the EH receptor in ambulacrarians, mollusks, annelids, nemerteans and phoronids suggests co-evolution of this ligand-receptor pair throughout Metazoa.
claims.source: The identification of the EH receptor in ambulacrarians, mollusks, annelids, nemerteans and phoronids suggests co-evolution of this ligand-receptor pair throughout Metazoa (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 4, Figure 2—source data 3).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the correlated distribution of EH ligand and receptor across metazoan lineages.

claims.claim: The eh-receptor gene was not found in Cnidaria, Xenacoelomorpha and Onychophora.
claims.source: Although the eh-receptor gene was not found in Cnidaria, Xenacoelomorpha and Onychophora, its distribution includes the Brachiopoda, Ectoprocta and Cephalochordata lineages.
claims.evidence: This is based on the genomic screening conducted in this study.

claims.claim: The eh-receptor distribution includes the Brachiopoda, Ectoprocta and Cephalochordata lineages.
claims.source: Although the eh-receptor gene was not found in Cnidaria, Xenacoelomorpha and Onychophora, its distribution includes the Brachiopoda, Ectoprocta and Cephalochordata lineages.
claims.evidence: This is based on the genomic screening conducted in this study.

claims.claim: The ancestry of the EH peptidergic pathway dates back to the cnidarian-bilaterian split.
claims.source: Consequently, our findings shift the ancestry of this peptidergic pathway back to the cnidarian-bilaterian split (Figures 2A and 4A).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the presence of EH in cnidarians and bilaterians.

claims.claim: Crustacean cardioactive peptide (CCAP) was first isolated from the shore crab Carcinus maenas.
claims.source: First isolated from the shore crab Carcinus maenas, crustacean cardioactive peptide (CCAP) is a highly conserved amidated neuropeptide that increases heart rate in crustaceans and insects (Stangier et al., 1987; Cheung et al., 1992; Lehman et al., 1993; Suggs et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to the original discovery and characterization of CCAP.

claims.claim: CCAP is a highly conserved amidated neuropeptide that increases heart rate in crustaceans and insects.
claims.source: First isolated from the shore crab Carcinus maenas, crustacean cardioactive peptide (CCAP) is a highly conserved amidated neuropeptide that increases heart rate in crustaceans and insects (Stangier et al., 1987; Cheung et al., 1992; Lehman et al., 1993; Suggs et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on CCAP function.

claims.claim: CCAP accelerates the frequency and amplitude of oviduct contractions in the locust Locusta migratoria.
claims.source: CCAP has multiple functions in addition to its cardioacceleratory activity, such as accelerating the frequency and amplitude of oviduct contractions in the locust Locusta migratoria (Donini et al., 2001) and regulating the release of digestive enzymes in the cockroach Periplaneta americana (Sakai et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Donini et al. (2001).

claims.claim: CCAP regulates the release of digestive enzymes in the cockroach Periplaneta americana.
claims.source: CCAP has multiple functions in addition to its cardioacceleratory activity, such as accelerating the frequency and amplitude of oviduct contractions in the locust Locusta migratoria (Donini et al., 2001) and regulating the release of digestive enzymes in the cockroach Periplaneta americana (Sakai et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sakai et al. (2006).

claims.claim: CCAP is important for ecdysis in crustaceans and insects where it initiates the stereotyped sequence of behaviours that mark the end of the pre-ecdysis stage.
claims.source: CCAP is important for ecdysis in crustaceans and insects where it initiates the stereotyped sequence of behaviours that mark the end of the pre-ecdysis stage (Gammie and Truman, 1997a; Gammie and Truman, 1997b; Phlippen et al., 2000; Arakane et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies on CCAP function in ecdysis.

claims.claim: Transgenic Drosophila larvae lacking CCAP neurons moult normally and only exhibit a prolonged pre-ecdysis behaviour.
claims.source: However, transgenic Drosophila larvae lacking CCAP neurons moult normally and only exhibit a prolonged pre-ecdysis behaviour (Clark et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Clark et al. (2004).

claims.claim: In the snail Lymnaea stagnalis, immunostaining revealed a dense network of CCAP-positive fibres that likely function to regulate parts of the feeding behaviour.
claims.source: In the snail Lymnaea stagnalis (Vehovszky et al., 2005), immunostaining revealed a dense network of CCAP-positive fibres that likely function to regulate parts of the feeding behaviour.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Vehovszky et al. (2005).

claims.claim: In the oyster Saccostrea glomerata and in the cuttlefish Sepia officinalis, in vivo bioassays and immunohistochemistry suggested that the CCAP signalling pathway is involved in reproduction.
claims.source: In the oyster Saccostrea glomerata (In et al., 2016) and in the cuttlefish Sepia officinalis (Endress et al., 2018), in vivo bioassays using synthesised neuropeptides and immunohistochemistry suggested that the CCAP signalling pathway is involved in reproduction (e.g., spawning, oocyte transport, egg-laying).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to In et al. (2016) and Endress et al. (2018).

claims.claim: Sepia CCAP has been shown to increase the tonus of the vena cava, demonstrating its role in the regulation of hemolymph circulation.
claims.source: Additionally, Sepia CCAP has been shown to increase the tonus of the vena cava, demonstrating its role in the regulation of hemolymph circulation (Endress et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Endress et al. (2018).

claims.claim: In both mollusks and arthropods, CCAP functions in feeding, reproduction and regulation of hemolymph circulation.
claims.source: These results indicate that in both, mollusks and arthropods, CCAP functions in feeding, reproduction and regulation of hemolymph circulation, suggesting that these may have been its ancestral roles.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the functional studies in mollusks and arthropods.

claims.claim: Feeding, reproduction and regulation of hemolymph circulation may have been the ancestral roles of CCAP.
claims.source: These results indicate that in both, mollusks and arthropods, CCAP functions in feeding, reproduction and regulation of hemolymph circulation, suggesting that these may have been its ancestral roles.
claims.evidence: This is speculated based on the conserved functions across mollusks and arthropods.

claims.claim: In arthropods, co-option of CCAP into the ecdysis pathway expanded its set of functions to include moulting.
claims.source: In arthropods, co-option of CCAP into the ecdysis pathway expanded this set of functions to include moulting.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the presence of CCAP in the ecdysis pathway in arthropods but not in mollusks.

claims.claim: The CCAP receptor is a G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) that was first described from the Drosophila genome.
claims.source: The CCAP receptor is a G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) that was first described from the Drosophila genome and subsequently identified in many other insects (Cazzamali et al., 2003; Arakane et al., 2008; Vogel et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies identifying and characterizing the CCAP receptor.

claims.claim: The CCAP receptor was subsequently identified in many other insects.
claims.source: The CCAP receptor is a G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) that was first described from the Drosophila genome and subsequently identified in many other insects (Cazzamali et al., 2003; Arakane et al., 2008; Vogel et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies identifying the CCAP receptor in insects.

claims.claim: The CCAP ligand is present in mollusks, annelids, arthropods and tardigrades.
claims.source: We confirm here the presence of a CCAP ligand in mollusks, annelids, arthropods and tardigrades, as stated earlier (Veenstra, 2010; Jékely, 2013; Mirabeau and Joly, 2013; Conzelmann et al., 2013; Stewart et al., 2014; Ahn et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2018; Koziol, 2018), and extend the distribution of the CCAP ligand to three additional lophotrochozoan phyla (Nemertea, Platyhelminthes and Rotifera) as well as to the remaining panarthropod phylum Onychophora (Figures 2B and 4B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, Figure 2—source data 4).
claims.evidence: This is based on the genomic screening conducted in this study and corroborated by previous studies.

claims.claim: The distribution of the CCAP ligand extends to three additional lophotrochozoan phyla (Nemertea, Platyhelminthes and Rotifera) as well as to the remaining panarthropod phylum Onychophora.
claims.source: We confirm here the presence of a CCAP ligand in mollusks, annelids, arthropods and tardigrades, as stated earlier (Veenstra, 2010; Jékely, 2013; Mirabeau and Joly, 2013; Conzelmann et al., 2013; Stewart et al., 2014; Ahn et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2018; Koziol, 2018), and extend the distribution of the CCAP ligand to three additional lophotrochozoan phyla (Nemertea, Platyhelminthes and Rotifera) as well as to the remaining panarthropod phylum Onychophora (Figures 2B and 4B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, Figure 2—source data 4).
claims.evidence: This is based on the genomic screening conducted in this study.

claims.claim: The CCAP ligand is absent from all investigated deuterostome genomes.
claims.source: Interestingly, the CCAP ligand is absent from all investigated deuterostome genomes analysed (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, Figure 2B, Figure 2—source data 4).
claims.evidence: This is based on the genomic screening conducted in this study.

claims.claim: The ccap-receptor ortholog was found in acoels, lophotrochozoans and panarthropods except Onychophora.
claims.source: The ccap-receptor ortholog was found in acoels, lophotrochozoans and panarthropods except Onychophora (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
claims.evidence: This is based on the phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claims.claim: The CCAP receptor was found in all deuterostome phyla (Echinodermata, Hemichordata, Vertebrata, Cephalochordata) except Tunicata.
claims.source: Surprisingly, we found the receptor also in all deuterostome phyla (Echinodermata, Hemichordata, Vertebrata, Cephalochordata) except Tunicata (Figure 2—figure supplement 5, Figure 2—source data 4).
claims.evidence: This is based on the phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claims.claim: The CCAP ligand-receptor pair originated at the base of Bilateria.
claims.source: These results reinforce the suggested origin of the ligand-receptor pair at the base of Bilateria and points towards a possible loss of the CCAP ligand in the Deuterostomia lineage (Figures 2B and 4A, Figure 2—figure supplement 5, Figure 2—source data 4).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the distribution of CCAP ligand and receptor across bilaterian lineages.

claims.claim: There was a possible loss of the CCAP ligand in the Deuterostomia lineage.
claims.source: These results reinforce the suggested origin of the ligand-receptor pair at the base of Bilateria and points towards a possible loss of the CCAP ligand in the Deuterostomia lineage (Figures 2B and 4A, Figure 2—figure supplement 5, Figure 2—source data 4).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the presence of the receptor but absence of the ligand in deuterostomes.

claims.claim: Bursicon was identified as a neurohormone responsible for cuticle sclerotization and melanisation (tanning) during post-ecdysis.
claims.source: Bursicon was identified as a neurohormone responsible for cuticle sclerotization and melanisation (tanning) during post-ecdysis (Cottrell, 1962a; Cottrell, 1962b; Fraenkel and Hsiao, 1965).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to the original studies identifying bursicon function.

claims.claim: Bursicon has a mild effect on the regulation of pre-ecdysis and is important for the proper execution of post-ecdysis in Manduca, Drosophila and Tribolium.
claims.source: Recent studies have shown that bursicon also has a mild effect on the regulation of pre-ecdysis and is important for the proper execution of post-ecdysis in Manduca, Drosophila and Tribolium as well as for the development of wings and other integumentary structures (Baker and Truman, 2002; Dewey et al., 2004; Arakane et al., 2008; Bai and Palli, 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on bursicon function in insects.

claims.claim: Bursicon is important for the development of wings and other integumentary structures.
claims.source: Recent studies have shown that bursicon also has a mild effect on the regulation of pre-ecdysis and is important for the proper execution of post-ecdysis in Manduca, Drosophila and Tribolium as well as for the development of wings and other integumentary structures (Baker and Truman, 2002; Dewey et al., 2004; Arakane et al., 2008; Bai and Palli, 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on bursicon function in insects.

claims.claim: Together with the ecdysis-triggering hormone signalling system, bursicon is an indispensable component of the moulting behaviour in insects.
claims.source: Together with the ecdydis-triggering hormone signalling system, bursicon is an indispensable component of the moulting behaviour in insects (Arakane et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Arakane et al. (2008).

claims.claim: Bursicon is present outside Ecdysozoa, for example in the anthozoan Nematostella vectensis, the echinoderm Strongylocentrotus purpuratus as well as in annelids and mollusks.
claims.source: Previous studies show that bursicon is present outside Ecdysozoa, for example in the anthozoan Nematostella vectensis, the echinoderm Strongylocentrotus purpuratus as well as in annelids and mollusks (Jékely, 2013; Conzelmann et al., 2013; Stewart et al., 2014; Ahn et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies identifying bursicon outside Ecdysozoa.

claims.claim: The distribution of bursicon (receptor and/or ligand) extends to the hemichordate, nemertean, phoronid, rotifer and onychophoran phyla.
claims.source: Our work confirms the presence of the complete bursicon signalling system in all arthropod genomes analysed here and extends its distribution (receptor and/or ligand) to the hemichordate, nemertean, phoronid, rotifer and onychophoran phyla (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, Figure 2—source data 5).
claims.evidence: This is based on the genomic screening conducted in this study.

claims.claim: Bursicon and its receptor rickets are absent in tardigrades.
claims.source: Interestingly, bursicon and its receptor rickets are absent in tardigrades, suggesting the loss of the bursicon peptidergic signalling in this lineage (Figures 2B and 4B, Figure 2—figure supplement 6, Figure 2—source data 5).
claims.evidence: This is based on the genomic screening conducted in this study.

claims.claim: The loss of the bursicon peptidergic signalling in tardigrades is suggested.
claims.source: Interestingly, bursicon and its receptor rickets are absent in tardigrades, suggesting the loss of the bursicon peptidergic signalling in this lineage (Figures 2B and 4B, Figure 2—figure supplement 6, Figure 2—source data 5).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the absence of bursicon and its receptor in tardigrades.

claims.claim: Independent proneuropeptide and peptide prohormone surveys in tardigrade genomic and EST data also failed to detect the bursicon ligand-receptor pair in different tardigrade species.
claims.source: The latter findings are corroborated by independent proneuropeptide and peptide prohormone surveys in the tardigrade genomic and EST data that also failed to detect this ligand-receptor pair in different tardigrade species (Christie et al., 2011; Koziol, 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to independent studies corroborating the absence of bursicon in tardigrades.

claims.claim: The bursicon receptor was not identified in any deuterostome or non-arthropod ecdysozoan lineage.
claims.source: We did not identify the receptor in any deuterostome or non-arthropod ecdysozoan lineage (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is based on the genomic screening conducted in this study.

claims.claim: The PTTH, ETH, EH, CCAP and bursicon peptide signalling systems are lacking in the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans.
claims.source: The PTTH, ETH, EH, CCAP and bursicon peptide signalling systems are lacking in the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans (cf. our study and, e.g., Page et al., 2014; Lažetić and Fay, 2017; Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on the genomic screening conducted in this study and corroborated by previous studies.

claims.claim: The ecdysteroid ecdysone (E), 20-hydroxyecdysone (20E), and various halloween gene products have been reported absent from the C. elegans genome.
claims.source: Additionally, other key moulting components, such as the ecdysteroid ecdysone (E), 20-hydroxyecdysone (20E), and various halloween gene products have also been reported absent from the C. elegans genome (Frand et al., 2005; Schumann et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on C. elegans moulting components.

claims.claim: An extensive body of research on moulting in C. elegans suggests an entirely different molecular machinery controlling this behaviour in this free-living nematode.
claims.source: An extensive body of research on moulting in C. elegans suggests an entirely different molecular machinery controlling this behaviour in this free-living nematode (Russel et al., 2011; for review Lažetić and Fay, 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to research on C. elegans moulting.

claims.claim: E and 20E were identified in parasitic nematodes.
claims.source: Interestingly, however, E and 20E were identified in parasitic nematodes (Cleator et al., 1987; Shea et al., 2004) and, outside Ecdysozoa, in the platyhelminth Monieza expansa, the gastropod mollusks Lymnaea stagnalis and Helix pomatia as well as in the hirudinean annelid Hirudo medicinalis (Mendis et al., 1984; Nolte et al., 1986; Garcia et al., 1989; Barker et al., 1990).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies identifying ecdysteroids in parasitic nematodes.

claims.claim: E and 20E were identified outside Ecdysozoa in the platyhelminth Monieza expansa, the gastropod mollusks Lymnaea stagnalis and Helix pomatia as well as in the hirudinean annelid Hirudo medicinalis.
claims.source: Interestingly, however, E and 20E were identified in parasitic nematodes (Cleator et al., 1987; Shea et al., 2004) and, outside Ecdysozoa, in the platyhelminth Monieza expansa, the gastropod mollusks Lymnaea stagnalis and Helix pomatia as well as in the hirudinean annelid Hirudo medicinalis (Mendis et al., 1984; Nolte et al., 1986; Garcia et al., 1989; Barker et al., 1990).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies identifying ecdysteroids in non-ecdysozoan taxa.

claims.claim: Key peptidergic components of the arthropod ecdysis pathway emerged prior to the protostome-deuterostome split.
claims.source: We show that key peptidergic components of the arthropod ecdysis pathway emerged prior to the protostome-deuterostome split, and thus considerably earlier than commonly assumed.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on the phyletic distribution data.

claims.claim: EH, CCAP and the bursicon signalling systems are more widespread among non-moulting animals than previously appreciated.
claims.source: EH, CCAP and the bursicon signalling systems are more widespread among non-moulting animals than previously appreciated.
claims.evidence: This is based on the identification of these components in non-ecdysozoan lineages.

claims.claim: The presence of the eth-receptor ortholog in ecdysozoans, lophotrochozoans and deuterostomes, in combination with the restriction of its known ligand to insects, arachnids and tardigrades, suggests a scenario in which promiscuous ligand/receptor relationships can lead to novel signalling interactions.
claims.source: The presence of the eth-receptor ortholog in ecdysozoans, lophotrochozoans and deuterostomes, in combination with the restriction of its known ligand to insects, arachnids and tardigrades, suggests a scenario in which promiscuous ligand/receptor relationships can lead to novel signalling interactions that provide new opportunities for natural selection to generate novel functions (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is speculated based on the distribution pattern of ETH ligand and receptor.

claims.claim: Promiscuous ligand/receptor relationships can provide new opportunities for natural selection to generate novel functions.
claims.source: The presence of the eth-receptor ortholog in ecdysozoans, lophotrochozoans and deuterostomes, in combination with the restriction of its known ligand to insects, arachnids and tardigrades, suggests a scenario in which promiscuous ligand/receptor relationships can lead to novel signalling interactions that provide new opportunities for natural selection to generate novel functions (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is a general evolutionary principle applied to the ETH system.

claims.claim: The identification of the near complete suite of the peptidergic arthropod ecdysis pathway components in Onychophora and Tardigrada strongly suggests that the entire pathway was at least functional in the last common ancestor of Panarthropoda.
claims.source: The identification of the near complete suite of the peptidergic arthropod ecdysis pathway components in Onychophora and Tardigrada strongly suggests that the entire pathway was at least functional in the last common ancestor of Panarthropoda and maybe as early as in the ur-ecdysozoan (Figures 2B and 4B).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the presence of most pathway components in onychophorans and tardigrades.

claims.claim: The entire ecdysis pathway may have been functional as early as in the ur-ecdysozoan.
claims.source: The identification of the near complete suite of the peptidergic arthropod ecdysis pathway components in Onychophora and Tardigrada strongly suggests that the entire pathway was at least functional in the last common ancestor of Panarthropoda and maybe as early as in the ur-ecdysozoan (Figures 2B and 4B).
claims.evidence: This is speculated based on the distribution of pathway components across ecdysozoan lineages.

claims.claim: ETH was apparently secondarily lost in Onychophora.
claims.source: However, considering the crucial role of the ETH and bursicon signalling systems in insect moulting, together with the apparent secondary loss of ETH in Onychophora and bursicon in Tardigrada (Figure 4B), the consequences of harbouring only the partial set of the ecdysis signalling genes should be the focus of future assessments.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the absence of ETH in onychophoran genomes despite its presence in other panarthropods.

claims.claim: Bursicon was apparently secondarily lost in Tardigrada.
claims.source: However, considering the crucial role of the ETH and bursicon signalling systems in insect moulting, together with the apparent secondary loss of ETH in Onychophora and bursicon in Tardigrada (Figure 4B), the consequences of harbouring only the partial set of the ecdysis signalling genes should be the focus of future assessments.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the absence of bursicon in tardigrade genomes despite its presence in other panarthropods.

claims.claim: Independent recruitment of novel peptidergic components into insect ecdysis has been shown.
claims.source: Independent recruitment of novel peptidergic components into insect ecdysis has been shown (cf. Kim et al., 2004; Kim et al., 2006a; Kim et al., 2006b; extensively reviewed by Zitnan et al., 1996), illustrating the evolutionary plasticity of this signalling pathway and calling for more detailed functional investigations into the role of individual components during moulting of the various ecdysozoan lineages.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies showing recruitment of new components.

claims.claim: The ecdysis signalling pathway exhibits evolutionary plasticity.
claims.source: Independent recruitment of novel peptidergic components into insect ecdysis has been shown (cf. Kim et al., 2004; Kim et al., 2006a; Kim et al., 2006b; extensively reviewed by Zitnan et al., 1996), illustrating the evolutionary plasticity of this signalling pathway and calling for more detailed functional investigations into the role of individual components during moulting of the various ecdysozoan lineages.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the independent recruitment of novel components.

claims.claim: 39 metazoan genomes and 57 transcriptomes were screened in this study.
claims.source: By screening 39 metazoan genomes and 57 transcriptomes (Supplementary file 1), we found that the PTTH peptide is present in Drosophila and Tribolium but absent in the house spider Parasteatoda tepidariorum and the crustacean Parhyale hawaiensis, suggesting that PTTH is an insect innovation (Figure 2A,B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, Figure 2—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This describes the scope of the genomic and transcriptomic data analyzed.

results.result: The study identifies trunk, a signaling molecule and paralog of insect PTTH, in the ctenophore Mnemiopsis leidyi, representing the first ctenophore signaling peptide with homology to a neuropeptide and extending the phyletic distribution of trunk to ctenophores.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C32, and C33 provide convergent evidence from similarity searches (p < 1e-05) and clustering analysis demonstrating trunk presence and homology in M. leidyi. The novelty claim (C10) and phyletic extension (C34) are well-supported by the data presented in Figures 2 and 3, with appropriate statistical thresholds and phylogenetic methods.

results.result: Eclosion hormone (EH) and bursicon originated prior to the cnidarian-bilaterian split, with the EH peptidergic pathway dating back to this evolutionary divergence.
results.evaluation: Claims C3 and C70 are supported by phylogenetic distribution data (C65) showing EH ligand presence in cnidarians and across bilaterian lineages (Figures 2A, 2B, 4A). The identification in cnidarians combined with broad bilaterian distribution provides strong evidence for pre-cnidarian-bilaterian origin.

results.result: ETH receptor and CCAP ligand-receptor pair originated in the bilaterian last common ancestor, with individual ETH signaling components present at the base of Bilateria.
results.evaluation: Claims are supported by phylogenetic analyses (C52, C85, C88, C89) showing ETH receptor and CCAP components across bilaterian lineages but absent in cnidarians. The presence of receptors in deuterostomes, lophotrochozoans, and ecdysozoans (Figures 2B, 4A) provides strong evidence for bilaterian origin.

results.result: The near-complete ecdysis pathway was present in the panarthropod last common ancestor, based on identification of EH, CCAP, and bursicon in Onychophora and EH, ETH, and CCAP in Tardigrada.
results.evaluation: Claims C5 and C6 are supported by genomic screening data (C117) identifying pathway components in onychophorans and tardigrades. The inference of pathway presence in the panarthropod LCA (C7, C111) is well-justified by the distribution pattern across panarthropod lineages shown in Figures 2B and 4B.

results.result: PTTH is an insect innovation, present in Drosophila and Tribolium but absent in non-insect arthropods including spiders and crustaceans.
results.evaluation: Claim C24 is based on screening 39 genomes and 57 transcriptomes (C117), with absence in spider and crustacean representatives. The inference of insect innovation (C25) is supported by the restricted distribution pattern, though limited taxonomic sampling of non-insect arthropods introduces some uncertainty.

results.result: The trunk-torso neuropeptide signaling pathway dates back to the last common ancestor of Cnidaria, Ctenophora, and Bilateria, extending trunk distribution to multiple new phyla and demonstrating the pathway is not restricted to Bilateria.
results.evaluation: Claims are supported by identification of trunk in onychophorans, tardigrades, and multiple other phyla (C29), and torso receptor across deuterostomes, lophotrochozoans, cnidarians, and ecdysozoans (C37). Phylogenetic analysis (Figure 2—supplement 2) supports ancient origin (C38, C39), contradicting previous bilaterian-restricted hypotheses.

results.result: The eth gene originated in the last common ancestor of Panarthropoda, with no orthologs identified outside panarthropods including C. elegans.
results.evaluation: Claim C50 is based on comprehensive genomic screening showing absence in non-panarthropod genomes. The inference of panarthropod origin (C51) is well-supported by the restricted distribution, though the absence of ETH in onychophorans (C48, C113) complicates this conclusion and suggests possible secondary loss.

results.result: EH ligand distribution extends to cnidarians, acoels, hemichordates, and multiple lophotrochozoan phyla, with conserved cysteine residues and co-evolution of the ligand-receptor pair throughout Metazoa.
results.evaluation: Claim C65 is supported by genomic screening data identifying EH in new lineages. Sequence analysis confirms conserved cysteines (C66), with cnidarians showing five instead of six. The correlated distribution of ligand and receptor (C67-C69) across metazoan lineages supports co-evolution, though receptor absence in some lineages (C68) suggests complexity.

results.result: CCAP ligand distribution extends to additional lophotrochozoan phyla and Onychophora, with the ligand absent from deuterostomes but the receptor present, suggesting possible loss of CCAP ligand in the Deuterostomia lineage.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C86 are supported by genomic screening extending CCAP distribution. The pattern of ligand absence (C87) but receptor presence (C89) in deuterostomes is well-documented in phylogenetic analyses (Figure 2—supplement 5). The inference of ligand loss in deuterostomes (C91) is reasonable but remains speculative without functional validation.

results.result: Bursicon distribution extends to hemichordate, nemertean, phoronid, rotifer, and onychophoran phyla, but is absent in tardigrades, suggesting loss of bursicon signaling in this lineage.
results.evaluation: Claim C97 is supported by genomic screening data. The absence in tardigrades (C98) is corroborated by independent studies (C100), strengthening the inference of secondary loss (C99). The restriction of the receptor to arthropods and lophotrochozoans (C101) is well-documented in phylogenetic analyses.

results.result: C. elegans lacks the PTTH, ETH, EH, CCAP, and bursicon peptide signaling systems as well as ecdysteroids and halloween genes, with an entirely different molecular machinery controlling moulting in this nematode.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C103 are supported by genomic screening and corroborated by previous studies. The inference of different molecular machinery (C104) is well-supported by extensive C. elegans research literature, though the claims primarily rely on absence of evidence rather than direct functional characterization.

results.result: ETH was apparently secondarily lost in Onychophora and bursicon was apparently secondarily lost in Tardigrada.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C114 infer secondary losses based on absence in genomic data (C48, C98). However, the authors acknowledge genome fragmentation issues for onychophorans (C49), limiting confidence in ETH loss. While bursicon absence is corroborated by independent studies (C100), the inference of secondary loss requires more complete genomic data and functional validation.

results.result: Key peptidergic components of the arthropod ecdysis pathway emerged prior to the protostome-deuterostome split, with EH, CCAP, and bursicon signaling systems more widespread among non-moulting animals than previously appreciated.
results.evaluation: These summary claims (C107-C108) are well-supported by the collective phylogenetic distribution data showing EH and bursicon in cnidarians (pre-bilaterian), and ETH receptor and CCAP in deuterostomes and lophotrochozoans. The comprehensive taxonomic sampling (C117) and multiple phylogenetic analyses provide strong evidence for ancient origins.

results.result: The signaling cascade underlying moulting differs between Panarthropoda and the remaining ecdysozoans.
results.evaluation: Claim C2 is supported by the differential distribution of pathway components, particularly the absence of key peptidergic systems in C. elegans (C102) versus their presence in panarthropods (C5-C7). The evidence from phylogenetic distribution and functional studies in different lineages supports this conclusion.

results.result: The presence of ETH receptor across ecdysozoans, lophotrochozoans, and deuterostomes, combined with ligand restriction to panarthropods, suggests promiscuous ligand/receptor relationships can lead to novel signaling interactions providing opportunities for functional evolution.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C110 present an evolutionary scenario based on the distribution pattern of ETH ligand and receptor (C52, C50). While the distribution data are solid, the inference about promiscuous ligand/receptor relationships and novel functions is speculative without experimental validation of receptor function in non-panarthropod lineages or identification of alternative ligands.

results.result: PTTH evolved from duplication of the ancient bilaterian signaling molecule-encoding gene trunk, which was previously identified in arthropods, annelids, mollusks, and cephalochordates.
results.evaluation: Claim C23 is supported by citations to previous studies proposing this evolutionary relationship. Claim C28 represents prior knowledge that is corroborated and extended by the current study's findings (C29). The clustering analysis (C33) further supports the paralogous relationship between PTTH and trunk.

results.result: PTTH ablation in Drosophila causes developmental delay, prolonged feeding, larger body size, and reduced fecundity, indicating PTTH regulates developmental timing and body size but is not essential for moulting.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C27 are based on cited experimental work (McBrayer et al., 2007). The interpretation that PTTH is not essential for moulting is reasonable given flies can still moult without it, though this represents prior work rather than new findings from the current study.

results.result: ETH knockdown in Drosophila, Tribolium, and Schistocerca leads to lethality at ecdysis onset, demonstrating the essential role of ETH signaling in moulting.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C44 are based on multiple cited experimental studies showing consistent lethal phenotypes across insect species. This represents well-established prior knowledge that provides functional context for the phylogenetic distribution findings, though it is not new data from the current study.

results.result: The essentiality of EH for moulting in Drosophila is contested, with one study showing non-essential role with behavioral deficits and another showing lethality in null mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C61 accurately represent conflicting results from prior studies (McNabb et al., 1997 vs. Krüger et al., 2015). The authors appropriately present both findings without resolving the contradiction, which is important context for interpreting the phylogenetic distribution of EH but does not represent new experimental work.

results.result: CCAP functions in feeding, reproduction, and hemolymph circulation in both mollusks and arthropods, suggesting these as ancestral roles, with co-option into the ecdysis pathway in arthropods expanding functions to include moulting.
results.evaluation: Claim C80 is supported by functional studies in mollusks and arthropods (C77-C79). However, the inference of ancestral roles (C81) and co-option scenario (C82) are speculative without functional studies in additional lineages or ancestral state reconstruction. The evolutionary interpretation requires more direct evidence.

results.result: Independent recruitment of novel peptidergic components into insect ecdysis has been demonstrated, illustrating evolutionary plasticity of the signaling pathway.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C116 are based on cited prior work showing recruitment of new components. This represents established knowledge about pathway evolution that provides important context for interpreting the current phylogenetic findings, though it is not new data from this study.

results.result: Arthropod ecdysis involves three stages (pre-ecdysis, ecdysis, post-ecdysis) controlled by a cascade of hormones and neuropeptides including PTTH, ecdysteroids, ETH, EH, CCAP, and bursicon in a sequential signaling pathway.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C20 describe the established insect ecdysis pathway based on prior literature (Figure 1). These represent well-documented background knowledge that provides essential context for the phylogenetic distribution study, though they are not new findings from the current work.

results.result: Ecdysteroids and biosynthesis genes are present outside Ecdysozoa in parasitic nematodes and various lophotrochozoans, indicating some moulting molecular players predate Ecdysozoa origin.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C22 and C105-C106 are based on cited biochemical studies identifying ecdysteroids in non-ecdysozoan taxa. This represents important prior knowledge about the ancient origins of moulting components, providing context for the peptidergic pathway findings, though it is not new data from this study.

results.result: Trunk ortholog was not found in Nematostella vectensis genome but is present in other anthozoans including Stylophora pistillata and Orbicella faveolata.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C31 are based on genomic screening and NCBI database searches. The absence in N. vectensis but presence in other anthozoans suggests either incomplete genome assembly or lineage-specific loss, though the authors do not extensively discuss this discrepancy.

results.result: ETH ligand was found only in insects among the arthropods screened, but previous studies show presence in chelicerates and crustaceans.
results.evaluation: Claim C46 accurately reports the screening results from this study, while C47 appropriately cites prior work showing broader arthropod distribution. The limited detection in this study likely reflects taxonomic sampling rather than true absence, as acknowledged by citing prior work.

results.result: The entire ETH signaling pathway was not found in onychophoran genomes, but genome fragmentation prevents definitive conclusions about loss in this lineage.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C49 appropriately report the absence of ETH in onychophoran genomes while acknowledging the limitation of fragmented assemblies. This cautious interpretation is scientifically appropriate given the data quality concerns, though it limits the strength of conclusions about ETH evolution.

results.result: There is substantial expansion of eth-receptor homologs in the genomes of Branchiostoma floridae and B. belcheri.
results.evaluation: Claim C53 is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2—supplement 3. The expansion is clearly visible in the phylogenetic tree, though the functional significance of this expansion is not explored and would require additional investigation.

results.result: The entire ecdysis pathway may have been functional as early as in the ur-ecdysozoan.
results.evaluation: Claim C112 extends the inference beyond the panarthropod LCA to the ecdysozoan ancestor. This is speculative given the absence of pathway components in C. elegans (C102) and limited sampling of other ecdysozoan lineages. The claim requires more comprehensive sampling across Nematoda, Scalidophora, and other ecdysozoan groups.

results.result: The study screened 39 metazoan genomes and 57 transcriptomes.
results.evaluation: Claim C117 describes the scope of data analyzed, which is documented in Supplementary file 1. This represents appropriate methodological reporting, though the specific taxonomic coverage and data quality vary across lineages, which may affect detection sensitivity.
